---
title: "How to predict brain regions"
---

Two published decoders give each recording channel one of 13 Cosmos-level brain regions,
from its electrophysiological features:

| decoder | Hugging Face repo | reads | agreement column |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ProbeTransformer** | [`int-brain-lab/ea-decoder-channel-transformer`](https://huggingface.co/int-brain-lab/ea-decoder-channel-transformer) | A whole probe at once, with depth along the probe | `seed_agreement`, over 5 seeds |
| **XGBoost** | [`int-brain-lab/ea-decoder-channel-xgboost`](https://huggingface.co/int-brain-lab/ea-decoder-channel-xgboost) | Each channel on its own | `fold_agreement`, over 5 folds |

The ProbeTransformer attends across all channels of a probe, using depth along the probe
(`axial_um`) as its positional signal, so a channel's prediction can use the channels
above and below it. The XGBoost decoder sees each channel independently.

This guide uses the ProbeTransformer. The XGBoost decoder takes the same table and returns
the same columns; [predict with XGBoost](#predict-with-xgboost) covers what differs.

If you have not loaded a model yet, start with
[how to download a published model](download-models.qmd).

## What the decoders need

```python
from ephysatlas import load_pretrained

transformer = load_pretrained(
    "int-brain-lab/ea-decoder-channel-transformer", revision="2026_W42"
)

print(transformer.inputs["index"])             # ['pid', 'channel']
print(len(transformer.inputs["features"]))     # 51
print(transformer.inputs["position_column"])   # axial_um
print(transformer.config["region_map"])        # Cosmos
```

Three requirements:

1. A DataFrame indexed by **`(pid, channel)`**.
2. Every column in `transformer.inputs["features"]`, plus the position column `axial_um`.
   `predict` raises `KeyError` naming any that are absent.
3. Features that are **aggregated and denoised** for this model's vintage — see
   [aggregate and denoise](aggregate-and-denoise.qmd). Denoising returns `rms_ap` and
   `rms_lf` in dB and `spike_count` (a rate, in spikes/s) in log2, and the decoders expect
   those units. `predict` cannot check this: a raw single-snippet table has the right
   column names and the wrong units, so it runs without an error and returns wrong regions.

## Prepare the table

The denoised table, `raw_ephys_features_denoised.pqt`, has every required column except
**`outside`**, a boolean derived from `channel_labels == 3` at read time rather than
stored. Passing the denoised table straight to `predict` raises:

```text
KeyError: "1 column(s) required by this model are missing from the input DataFrame:
['outside']. Expected the features plus the 'axial_um' position column."
```

This holds for the published `ea_active/2026_W42` aggregate and for a table computed
locally with [`compute_denoised_features`](compute-features-spikeglx.qmd#compute-features).

There are three ways to get a complete table. For a downloaded vintage, the simplest is the
pre-merged file, which already contains `outside`:

```python
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

path_features = Path("/data/features/ea_active/2026_W42/agg_full")   # from download_tables

df = pd.read_parquet(path_features / "df_all_cols_merged.pqt")
```

Or let `read_features_from_disk` derive it:

```python
import ephysatlas.data, ephysatlas.anatomy

df = ephysatlas.data.read_features_from_disk(
    path_features, brain_atlas=ephysatlas.anatomy.ClassifierAtlas()
)
```

Or derive it yourself, with no atlas download:

```python
df = pd.read_parquet(path_features / "raw_ephys_features_denoised.pqt")
df["outside"] = df["channel_labels"] == 3
```

## Predict with the ProbeTransformer {#predict}

```python
out = transformer.predict(df)

print(out[["predicted_acronym", "prediction_probability", "seed_agreement"]].head())
```

`out` is indexed like `df`, one row per channel. Channels with any non-finite feature are
dropped with a warning, so `out` can have fewer rows than `df`.

A real run on one probe of `ea_active/2026_W42` (`00a824c0-e060-495f-9ebc-79c82fef4c67`,
384 channels, all returned):

```text
predicted_acronym
MB            201
Isocortex     128
void           29
void_fluid     19
HPF             7

mean prob 0.816   mean seed_agreement 0.902
```

To try it with no data of your own, use the example the model ships, 768 channels from two
probes:

```python
sample = transformer.path_model / "example" / "features_sample.parquet"
out = transformer.predict(pd.read_parquet(sample))
```

## Reading the output

| column | meaning |
|---|---|
| `predicted_acronym` | Winning region as an Allen acronym |
| `predicted_atlas_id` | The same region as a numeric Allen structure id |
| `prediction_probability` | Probability of the winning class, averaged over the seed models |
| `seed_agreement` | Fraction of seed models that voted for the winner |
| `p_<acronym>` | One column per class, averaged over the seed models |

The XGBoost decoder returns the same columns, averaged over its fold models, with
`fold_agreement` in place of `seed_agreement`.

Both `2026_W42` decoders predict the same 13 **Cosmos**-level classes:

```python
print(transformer.config["class_acronyms"])
# ['void', 'MB', 'Isocortex', 'CB', 'TH', 'CNU', 'OLF', 'CTXsp', 'root', 'HB',
#  'HPF', 'HY', 'void_fluid']
```

Note that `void` and `void_fluid` are real classes: the model can say a channel is outside
brain tissue, which is useful for finding where a probe entered and exited.

### Two different kinds of uncertainty

`prediction_probability` and `seed_agreement` answer different questions:

| probability | agreement | interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| high | high | Confident and consistent — trust it |
| low | high | Every seed agrees this channel is ambiguous, likely a region boundary |
| low | low | The seeds disagree; the model has no coherent answer here |
| high | low | Rare and suspicious — inspect the channel |

For the XGBoost decoder, read the folds for the seeds.

```python
# Keep only channels the ensemble agrees on
confident = out[(out["prediction_probability"] > 0.5) & (out["seed_agreement"] >= 0.8)]
print(f"{len(confident)} / {len(out)} channels confidently assigned")
```

Filter on these two columns before using the predictions. On the probe above, 314 of the
384 channels pass this filter.

### The full probability distribution

The `p_<acronym>` columns give the whole posterior, not just the winner:

```python
prob_cols = [c for c in out.columns if c.startswith("p_")]
print(out[prob_cols].head())

# Runner-up per channel — often the anatomically adjacent region
top2 = out[prob_cols].apply(
    lambda r: r.nlargest(2).index[1].removeprefix("p_"), axis=1
)
```

## Predict with XGBoost {#predict-with-xgboost}

The XGBoost decoder predicts each channel from its own features alone. It takes the same
table:

```python
xgb = load_pretrained(
    "int-brain-lab/ea-decoder-channel-xgboost", revision="2026_W42"
)

print(len(xgb.inputs["features"]))   # 48
print(xgb.config["accuracy"])        # 0.6124

out_xgb = xgb.predict(df)
print(out_xgb[["predicted_acronym", "prediction_probability", "fold_agreement"]].head())
```

What differs from the ProbeTransformer:

- Its 48 features include `channel_labels` but not the four spike-shape columns
  (`spike_width_secs`, `predepolarisation_width_secs`, `spike_amplitude`,
  `peak_to_trough_ratio_log`), and it does not need `axial_um`.
- It returns every row: `out_xgb` is indexed exactly like `df`.
- The release ships five cross-validation fold models plus one model trained on all
  channels, so the agreement column is **`fold_agreement`**.
- It can denoise raw aggregated features inside `predict` (below).

On the same probe (352 of 384 channels pass the confidence filter above):

```text
predicted_acronym
MB            197
Isocortex     138
void           28
HPF            13
void_fluid      8

mean prob 0.779   mean fold_agreement 0.930
```

Its manifest records a held-out accuracy of 0.61 across the 13 classes. The accuracy is not
the same for every region. The confusion matrix shows which regions are reliable and what
the others are mistaken for:

![How often the region decoder predicts each region (columns) for each histology region (rows), normalised per row. Isocortex, midbrain (MB) and hippocampus (HPF) are mostly right; the cortical subplate (CTXsp) and hypothalamus (HY) are often called as a neighbour.](../figures/decoder_confusion_matrix.png){.lightbox width=70%}

Its shipped example holds 500 channels from 393 probes:

```python
sample = xgb.path_model / "example" / "features_sample.parquet"
out_xgb = xgb.predict(pd.read_parquet(sample))
```

On macOS, run the two decoders in separate processes or with `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`: see
[troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

### Denoising inside predict

If your table holds *raw* aggregated features, the XGBoost decoder can denoise them for
you:

```python
out_xgb = xgb.predict(df_raw, denoise=True)
```

Leave `denoise=False` (the default) when your features are already denoised. Denoising
twice degrades them. The ProbeTransformer has no such option.

Prefer denoising up front with
[`produce_output_dataframes`](aggregate-and-denoise.qmd): you get the denoised table on
disk for inspection, and you can reuse it across models.

## Ensemble or global

Both decoders ship several models and average them by default. `estimator=` picks between
the average and a single model:

```python
out = transformer.predict(df, estimator="ensemble")   # default
out = transformer.predict(df, estimator="global")
```

| | `"ensemble"` (default) | `"global"` |
|---|---|---|
| ProbeTransformer | Averages the 5 seed models | The first seed alone |
| XGBoost | Averages the 5 fold models | The single model trained on all channels |
| Cost | 5 forward passes | 1 forward pass |
| Agreement column | Real value in [0, 1] | `NaN` |

The agreement column is `NaN` for `global`: a single model has nothing to agree with, and
`1.0` would suggest that all the models agreed when only one was used. For XGBoost, the
ensemble is also slightly better calibrated.

::: {.callout-important}
The two estimators disagree on some channels: 9.6 % for the ProbeTransformer and 3.9 % for
XGBoost on the probe above. Use the same estimator throughout an analysis.
:::

## Joining predictions onto your data

Prediction columns are namespaced so the join is always safe:

```python
joined = df.join(out)
```

Both the channel feature table and the cluster table already carry histology-derived
`acronym` and `atlas_id` columns. Bare output names would collide on join and overwrite
the histology columns on assignment without a warning. `predicted_acronym` /
`predicted_atlas_id` cannot.

To compare the predictions with histology, you need a table that carries it: the pre-merged
file or the output of `read_features_from_disk`, not the denoised table alone. Their
`acronym` and `atlas_id` columns are Allen regions, while the decoders predict Cosmos
regions, so compare against `Cosmos_id`:

```python
labelled = df.join(out, how="inner")   # inner: out can have fewer rows than df
match = labelled["predicted_atlas_id"] == labelled["Cosmos_id"]
print(f"agreement with histology: {match.mean():.1%}")
```

## Plotting the result

`plot_cumulative_probas` draws the full posterior as stacked bands down the probe, in
Allen region colours:

![The two example probes of the ProbeTransformer: for each, the histology, the predicted region and the posterior as stacked bands. [Region predictions along the probe](../visualise/predictions-along-probe.qmd) has the code of this figure.](../figures/predictions_along_probe.png){.lightbox}

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import ephysatlas.plots
from ephysatlas.anatomy import NEW_VOID, ClassifierRegions

# The class list includes void_fluid (id 2000), unknown to plain BrainRegions
regions = ClassifierRegions()
regions.add_new_region(NEW_VOID)

# One probe at a time, sorted by depth. Join first: out can have fewer rows than df
pid = out.index.get_level_values("pid")[0]
probe = df[["axial_um"]].join(out, how="inner").xs(pid, level="pid").sort_values("axial_um")

# The p_<acronym> columns are in class order, so they align with config["classes"]
prob_cols = [f"p_{a}" for a in transformer.config["class_acronyms"]]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3, 8))
ephysatlas.plots.plot_cumulative_probas(
    probas=probe[prob_cols].to_numpy(),
    depths=probe["axial_um"].to_numpy(),
    aids=np.asarray(transformer.config["classes"]),   # one id per class, not per channel
    regions=regions,
    ax=ax,
    legend=True,
)
ax.set(xlabel="cumulative probability", ylabel="depth (µm)")
plt.show()
```

Three things to get right here: `aids` is one atlas id per **class** (13 of them), not one
per channel; `ax` must be supplied — the function draws onto the axes you give it and
returns it; and `regions` must know `void_fluid`, or its band is missing from the plot (the
default is plain `BrainRegions`).

See [plotting features along the probe](../visualise/features-along-probe.qmd) for the
depth-resolved feature view beside the predictions, and
[region predictions along the probe](../visualise/predictions-along-probe.qmd) for the
comparison with histology.

## Troubleshooting

**`KeyError` listing feature columns** — your table is missing those columns. Usually a
feature family you did not compute; the `2026_W42` decoders need all four (`lf`, `csd`,
`ap`, `waveforms`), and `waveforms` needs the `[full]` extra. A list of
`peak_val`, `trough_val`, `peak_time_secs` and friends means the opposite mismatch: an
older model on a table from `ephysatlas` 0.9.0 or later, which no longer has those
columns. Use the `2026_W42` model. A list of `*_bpr` columns means a table computed
before `ephysatlas` 0.10.0, whose first-difference columns are `*_csd_diff1`; recompute
the features.

**`ValueError` about the feature-order digest** — the manifest's feature list no longer
matches its recorded hash, meaning the model directory has been edited. Re-download it.

**Predictions look uniformly wrong** — check three things in order: `model.selftest()`
passes; your features are denoised; the feature vintage matches
`model.index["vintage"]`.

**Everything predicted `void` or `root`** — often a sign the input is raw rather than
denoised, so the feature values sit far outside the training distribution.

**`transformer.predict` never returns after the XGBoost decoder ran in the same process
(macOS)** — XGBoost and PyTorch each load their own OpenMP runtime, and the second one
deadlocks. Importing `torch` first instead crashes the XGBoost predict. Start Python with
`OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` (`OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 python my_script.py`), or run the two decoders in
separate processes. Seen with XGBoost 3.4.1 and PyTorch 2.14 on Apple Silicon.
